CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER

Calculating with natural numbers

You already know plus, minus, times and divided by from primary school. Now you learn to calculate cleverly: with laws that save you work, with an estimate that reveals mistakes at once, and with powers, a short way of writing long products. Finally it is about dividing, in your head and on paper, even when there is a remainder.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS4 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • use the terms sum, difference, product and quotient correctly
  • calculate cleverly with the commutative, the associative and the distributive law
  • make an estimate before calculating
  • read and calculate powers, know the square numbers up to $20^2$ and apply the order of operations
  • divide, in your head and on paper, with a remainder and with a check

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Laws of arithmetic and shortcuts

With $25 + 38 + 75 + 62$ you group cleverly: $25 + 75 = 100$ and $38 + 62 = 100$, together 200. With $4 \cdot 17 \cdot 25$ you first calculate $4 \cdot 25 = 100$ and then $100 \cdot 17 = 1700$. The laws of arithmetic say that you may rearrange like this.

Every calculation and its result have a name:

OperationCalculationResult
Additionaddend + addendsum
Subtractionminuend − subtrahenddifference
Multiplicationfactor · factorproduct
Divisiondividend ÷ divisorquotient
KEY POINT · THE LAWS OF ARITHMETIC

Commutative law (swapping): $a + b = b + a$ and $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$

Associative law (grouping): $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ and $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$

Distributive law (multiplying out): $a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c$, and the same with minus.

For subtraction and division the commutative and associative laws do not hold: $8 - 3 \neq 3 - 8$.

Letters instead of numbers: $a$, $b$ and $c$ stand for any numbers. That way you can write down a law for all numbers at once.

Estimate: Round the numbers so that you can calculate in your head. $398 \cdot 21 \approx 400 \cdot 20 = 8000$. If the exact calculation gives 835, something is wrong.

EXAMPLE 1 · DISTRIBUTIVE LAW

Calculate cleverly: a) $7 \cdot 102$   b) $13 \cdot 48 + 13 \cdot 52$

a) $7 \cdot (100 + 2) = 700 + 14 =$ 714

b) $13 \cdot (48 + 52) = 13 \cdot 100 =$ 1300

EXAMPLE 2 · FILLING A GAP

Which number belongs in the gap? $b + 27 = 64$

We are looking for the number to which you add 27 to get 64. The inverse helps: $64 - 27 = 37$.

$b = 37$, check: $37 + 27 = 64$

a) 52   b) 100   c) 7   d) for example $7 \cdot 8$, $1 \cdot 56$, $2 \cdot 28$, $4 \cdot 14$

a) $600 \cdot 50 = 30{,}000$; exactly 29,988   b) $4{,}000 + 6{,}000 = 10{,}000$; exactly 10,008   c) $8{,}000 - 3{,}000 = 5{,}000$; exactly 5,116

Lea claims: “With subtraction you may move brackets too.” Check with $(20 - 8) - 3$ and $20 - (8 - 3)$. How should you calculate $20 - 8 - 3$ cleverly?

$(20 - 8) - 3 = 9$, but $20 - (8 - 3) = 15$: Lea is wrong. Correct is $20 - 8 - 3 = 20 - (8 + 3) = 9$: subtracting two numbers one after the other means subtracting their sum.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Powers and the order of operations

On the chessboard the number of grains doubles from square to square. On the 10th square there are $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 512$ grains, nine twos multiplied together. More briefly you write $2^9$. On the 20th square there are already $2^{19} = 524{,}288$ grains.

A product of factors that are all the same is written as a power. The raised number says how often the factor occurs.

KEY POINT · POWERS

$$2^5 = \underbrace{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2}_{5\text{ factors}} = 32$$

The 2 is called the base, the 5 the exponent. You read “two to the power of five”. $a^2$ is also read “$a$ squared”.

Powers of ten: $10^1 = 10$, $10^2 = 100$, $10^3 = 1000$, $10^6 = 1{,}000{,}000$. The exponent counts the zeros.

KEY POINT · ORDER OF OPERATIONS
  1. Whatever is in brackets is calculated first.
  2. Then the powers.
  3. Then multiplication and division before addition and subtraction.
  4. Otherwise you calculate from left to right.

Careful: $2^5$ is not $2 \cdot 5$. It is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 32$.

You should know the square numbers up to 20 by heart: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, 169, 196, 225, 256, 289, 324, 361, 400.

INTERACTIVE · POWERS FROM CUBES

Set all three edges to the same length, for example 3: the cube consists of $3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 3^3 = 27$ small cubes. One layer on its own has $3^2 = 9$.

EXAMPLE 3 · CALCULATING POWERS

Calculate a) $3^4$   b) $15^2$   c) $10^5$   d) $1^{100}$

a) $3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 81$   b) $225$   c) $100{,}000$   d) $1$

EXAMPLE 4 · ORDER OF OPERATIONS

Calculate $50 - 2 \cdot (3 + 4)^2 \div 7$.

Brackets: $3 + 4 = 7$. Power: $7^2 = 49$. Multiplication and division from the left: $2 \cdot 49 = 98$, $98 \div 7 = 14$. Then subtraction: $50 - 14$.

36

Which square number lies between 150 and 180? Between which two square numbers does 300 lie?

$13^2 = 169$. 300 lies between $17^2 = 289$ and $18^2 = 324$.

Calculate $1$, $1 + 3$, $1 + 3 + 5$, $1 + 3 + 5 + 7$. What do you notice? What is the sum of the first 20 odd numbers? Draw a picture made of squares for the first sums.

Put an L-shape of squares round a square made of squares.

1, 4, 9, 16: you get the square numbers. Every odd number is an L-shape that makes the square one row bigger. The first 20 odd numbers give $20^2 = 400$.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Dividing, with and without a remainder

27 people in rooms of 4: $27 \div 4 = 6$ remainder 3, because $6 \cdot 4 = 24$ and 3 are left over. So six rooms are not enough; the class needs 7 rooms. There are 28 beds there, and one stays free.

Dividing is the inverse of multiplying: $56 \div 8 = 7$, because $7 \cdot 8 = 56$. With this you can test every division with a check. If a division does not work out exactly, there is a remainder. It is always smaller than the divisor.

KEY POINT · WRITTEN DIVISION

You work from left to right: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down the next digit, and start again.

952÷ 7 = 136
−7
25
−21
42
−42
0

Check: $136 \cdot 7 = 952$. With a remainder: $957 \div 7 = 136$ remainder 5, check $136 \cdot 7 + 5 = 957$.

You do not divide by 0. $6 \div 0$ would have to be a number that gives 6 when multiplied by 0. There is no such number, because everything times 0 is 0.

Zero divided: $0 \div 6 = 0$, because $0 \cdot 6 = 0$. That is allowed.

EXAMPLE 5 · IN YOUR HEAD

Calculate $84 \div 6$ in your head.

Split into parts that divide exactly: $84 = 60 + 24$, so $60 \div 6 + 24 \div 6 = 10 + 4$.

14, check $14 \cdot 6 = 84$

EXAMPLE 6 · WORD PROBLEM WITH A REMAINDER

500 eggs are packed in boxes of ten; the first 6 eggs are broken. How many full boxes are there?

$494 \div 10 = 49$ remainder 4. The 4 eggs are not enough for another box.

49 full boxes, 4 eggs are left over.

a) 12   b) 13   c) 13   d) 800

Divide on paper: a) $744 \div 6$   b) $918 \div 9$   c) $635 \div 5$   d) $860 \div 4$

Divide with a remainder and check: a) $100 \div 7$   b) $500 \div 3$   c) $999 \div 8$

a) 14 remainder 2 ($14 \cdot 7 + 2 = 100$)   b) 166 remainder 2   c) 124 remainder 7

A coach has 52 seats. 340 pupils are going to a concert. How many coaches are needed? How many seats stay free?

$340 \div 52 = 6$ remainder 28: 7 coaches; $7 \cdot 52 - 340 = 24$ seats stay free.

Find the mistake and calculate correctly: Tom calculates $824 \div 4 = 26$.

Make an estimate: $800 \div 4$.

The estimate is 200, so 26 cannot be right. Tom forgot the zero: after $8 \div 4 = 2$ comes $2 \div 4 = 0$ remainder 2, then $24 \div 4 = 6$. The correct answer is 206.

If you divide a number by 7, the remainder is 3. If you divide it by 5, it works out exactly. Find the smallest such number and one more.

Try the multiples of 5: 10 = 1 · 7 + 3. The next one is $10 + 35 = 45$, because $45 = 6 \cdot 7 + 3$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Calculate $65 \div 5$.

$13 \cdot 5 = 65$

What remainder is left with $90 \div 7$?

$12 \cdot 7 = 84$, remainder 6

27 people, 4 per room. What is the smallest number of rooms needed?

$27 \div 4 = 6$ remainder 3, so one more room.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Calculate: a) $(17 + 23) \cdot 5$   b) $17 + 23 \cdot 5$   c) $2^3 + 3^2$   d) $144 \div 12 - 12$

a) 200   b) 132   c) 17   d) 0

Connecting with chapter 1.1: Write in digits and in words: a) $10^7$   b) $10^{12}$. How many zeros does a googol, i.e. $10^{100}$, have?

a) 10,000,000, ten million   b) 1,000,000,000,000, a trillion. A googol has 100 zeros.

A cinema has 18 rows with 24 seats each. For one showing 389 tickets have been sold. How many seats are free? Write the calculation as one expression with brackets.

$(18 \cdot 24) - 389 = 432 - 389 = 43$ free seats. You may also leave the brackets out, because multiplication comes before subtraction.

How many grains lie on the first 5 squares of the chessboard together? On the first 10? Compare each time with the number on the next square. What do you suspect?

$1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31$; the next square has 32. The first 10 squares: 1023; the 11th square has 1024. Conjecture: all the squares up to a square together always have exactly one grain fewer than the next square.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Young Gauss calculates fast

Carl Friedrich Gauss, born in 1777 in Braunschweig, became one of the greatest mathematicians of all time. Later this story was told about his time at school: the teacher Büttner gave the class a long addition problem so as to have some peace for a while. After a short time the nine-year-old Gauss put his slate on the desk. Only the result was on it, and it was correct.

Usually the problem is told like this: add all the numbers from 1 to 100. Gauss is said to have calculated like this: $1 + 100 = 101$, $2 + 99 = 101$, $3 + 98 = 101$, and so on up to $50 + 51 = 101$. That is 50 pairs with the sum 101, so $50 \cdot 101 = 5050$. He used the commutative and the associative law without thinking about it for long.

Try it yourself: what is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 1000?

Sources: W. Sartorius von Waltershausen: Gauß zum Gedächtniss. Hirzel, Leipzig 1856. B. Hayes: Gauss's Day of Reckoning. American Scientist 94 (2006), pp. 200–205. Sartorius does not say exactly how Gauss calculated. The version with the numbers 1 to 100 and the pairs only appeared in later retellings.

Solution: 500 pairs with the sum 1001 give 500,500.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

TERMS

sum, difference, product, quotient

$96 \div 8 = 12$: dividend 96, divisor 8, quotient 12

LAWS OF ARITHMETIC

Swapping and grouping with plus and times, multiplying out: $a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c$

$7 \cdot 102 = 700 + 14 = 714$

POWERS

Base to the power of the exponent: the exponent counts the equal factors

$2^5 = 32$ · $10^6 = 1{,}000{,}000$

ORDER OF OPERATIONS

Brackets before powers before multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, otherwise from left to right

$50 - 2 \cdot (3 + 4)^2 \div 7 = 36$

DIVIDING

Inverse of multiplication, remainder smaller than the divisor, check

$957 \div 7 = 136$ remainder 5
